lead: A decoder takes an n-bit code and activates exactly one of 2ⁿ output lines. A multiplexer does the opposite job: it selects one of many data inputs and sends it to a single output. A comparator takes two words and decides whether they are equal, or which is larger. These three blocks route and judge data inside adders, memories and processors. A decoder drives a memory wordline, a multiplexer chooses between results, and a comparator makes a branch decision.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for XOR and equality, and pass transistor logic and transmission gates for the multiplexer switches.

sections.h3: Decoder: a code in, one line out

blocks.text: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder has n input bits and 2ⁿ output lines. For each input code exactly one output is active. A 3-to-8 decoder takes inputs A, B, C, where A is the most significant bit. Input ABC = 101 activates output Y5, because binary 101 equals decimal 5.

Inside is an AND plane. Each input bit drives an inverter, so both true and complement are available. Output Y<sub>i</sub> is an n-input AND of the chosen literals. For the 3-to-8 decoder, Y5 = A·B′·C. The decoder is a minterm generator: output i is minterm m<sub>i</sub>. Active-high means the selected line is 1. Active-low means it is 0; a NAND plane or an output inverter gives that.
Here Y<sub>i</sub> is output line i; b<sub>n−1</sub>…b<sub>0</sub> is the input code; i is the line number from 0 to 2ⁿ−1.

An enable input turns the whole decoder on or off. Larger decoders use enables to combine smaller ones. A 3-to-8 decoder can be two 2-to-4 decoders: A enables the upper half when A=1 and the lower half when A=0; B and C select the line inside each half. In a memory, a row decoder drives one wordline high for the addressed row (Chapter 4.10). The delay is about one inverter delay plus one n-input AND delay.

sections.h3: Multiplexer: many lines in, one out

blocks.text: A 2:1 multiplexer has data inputs D0 and D1, select S, and output Y. Y equals D0 when S=0 and D1 when S=1, so Y = S′·D0 + S·D1. A pass-transistor pair can build it with two transistors. A transmission gate uses an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, so both 0 and 1 pass without a threshold drop (see pass transistor logic and transmission gates).

A mux tree builds wider multiplexers. A 4:1 mux uses three 2:1 muxes: the first stage selects D0/D1 and D2/D3 with S0, the second stage selects between those two results with S1. An 8:1 mux uses seven 2:1 muxes and three select levels. For an N:1 mux tree the number of select levels is ceil(log₂N), so t<sub>pd</sub> ≈ ceil(log₂N) × t<sub>mux</sub>.

Shannon expansion makes the mux a logic element. Any function f(x1,…,xn) = x1·f(1,…) + x1′·f(0,…). Use the select lines as the variables and tie each data input to 0 or 1, or to a remaining function. An 8:1 mux with selects A,B,C and data inputs equal to the truth table implements any f(A,B,C). A tristate buffer adds a high-impedance state, so many drivers can share a bus; enable exactly one driver at a time.

A 1-bit equality gate is an XNOR: E = A·B + A′·B′. It gives 1 when the two bits are equal. For n bits, E = E<sub>n−1</sub>·…·E<sub>0</sub>. This is an AND tree. A linear AND chain has delay t<sub>XNOR</sub> + (n−1)·t<sub>AND</sub>; a balanced tree has delay t<sub>XNOR</sub> + ceil(log₂n)·t<sub>AND</sub>.

The magnitude cell compares one bit pair and carries the decision. It has inputs A<sub>i</sub>, B<sub>i</sub> and incoming G<sub>in</sub>, L<sub>in</sub>, E<sub>in</sub>. G means A>B so far, L means A<B so far, E means equal so far. Outputs are: G<sub>out</sub> = G<sub>in</sub> + E<sub>in</sub>·A<sub>i</sub>·B<sub>i</sub>′ ; L<sub>out</sub> = L<sub>in</sub> + E<sub>in</sub>·A<sub>i</sub>′·B<sub>i</sub> ; E<sub>out</sub> = E<sub>in</sub>·(A<sub>i</sub> XNOR B<sub>i</sub>). Where G<sub>out</sub>, L<sub>out</sub>, E<sub>out</sub> are the updated flags; + is OR; · is AND; ′ is NOT.

Start at the MSB with G<sub>in</sub>=0, L<sub>in</sub>=0, E<sub>in</sub>=1. Feed each cell's outputs to the next less significant cell. The first differing bit decides, and later bits cannot change it. After the last cell, G<sub>out</sub>=1 means A>B, L<sub>out</sub>=1 means A<B, and E<sub>out</sub>=1 means A=B. The chain has n cells, so delay is about n × t<sub>cell</sub>. Reading from the LSB end is wrong because a later MSB difference must override the earlier answer.

spec.aria: Decoder with outputs Y1, Y2, Y5 and Y7 wired to an OR gate; four comparator cells for 1011 against 1010 ending with G equals 1.

examples.question: A logic function is f(A,B,C)=Σm(1,2,5,7). (a) Implement it with a 3-to-8 decoder and one OR gate. (b) Compare A=1011₂ (11) with B=1010₂ (10) using the magnitude-cell chain from the MSB. Give the final G, L, E flags.
steps: The 3-to-8 decoder outputs Y0..Y7, with Y<sub>i</sub>=m<sub>i</sub>. For the given function the needed minterms are 1, 2, 5, 7.
Tie Y1, Y2, Y5, Y7 to a 4-input OR gate. Output f=Y1+Y2+Y5+Y7. f=1 for ABC=001, 010, 101, 111 and 0 otherwise.
Compare bit 3 (MSB): A3=1, B3=1. Equal, so E=1, G=0, L=0.
Bit 2: A2=0, B2=0. Equal remains E=1.
Bit 1: A1=1, B1=1. Equal remains E=1.
Bit 0: A0=1, B0=0. Here A<sub>i</sub>=1 and B<sub>i</sub>=0, so the cell sets G<sub>out</sub>=1, L<sub>out</sub>=0, E<sub>out</sub>=0.
examples.answer: f = Σm(1,2,5,7) using Y1+Y2+Y5+Y7; for 1011 vs 1010, the final flags are G=1, L=0, E=0, so A>B.

traps: Treating active-low decoder outputs as active-high: an active-low selected line is 0, so ORing selected lines does not give the sum of minterms; use NAND or invert.
Building a large decoder from smaller ones without using the enable as the extra address bit; the MSB must enable the correct half.
Letting a comparator decide from the LSB end. The first differing MSB decides, and later bits cannot override it.
Forgetting that a tristate bus needs exactly one enabled driver: two drivers cause contention, none causes a floating bus.
Confusing a multiplexer's select lines with its data inputs in Shannon expansion, or tying a data input to a variable that is also a select.

quiz.a: It has n input bits and 2ⁿ outputs. For each input code exactly one output is active, so output i is active when the input code equals i.

quiz.q: Why does a decoder use inverters on its inputs?
quiz.a: Each output is an AND of true or complemented input bits. Inverters make both polarities available, so every minterm can be formed.

quiz.q: Use a 3-to-8 decoder and one OR gate to implement f(A,B,C)=Σm(0,3,6). Which decoder outputs go to the OR gate?
quiz.a: The minterms are 0, 3 and 6, so tie Y0, Y3 and Y6 to the OR gate. The output is f=Y0+Y3+Y6.

quiz.q: Compare A=1100₂ (12) with B=1011₂ (11) from the MSB down. Which bit decides, and what are G, L, E?
quiz.a: Bit 3: 1 vs 1, equal. Bit 2: A=1, B=0, so this bit decides. Final flags: G=1, L=0, E=0, so A>B.

quiz.q: Why must a magnitude comparator chain run from the MSB to the LSB?
quiz.a: The most significant differing bit decides the comparison. A less significant bit cannot override it. A chain that starts at the LSB would need extra logic to let later MSB differences override earlier decisions.

quiz.q: A 16:1 multiplexer is built from 2:1 multiplexers. How many 2:1 muxes are needed, and how many select levels are in the longest path?
quiz.a: A 16:1 mux needs 15 2:1 muxes: 8 in the first stage, 4, 2, then 1. It has 4 select levels, so the delay is about 4 × t<sub>mux</sub>.

quiz.q: An 8:1 mux has select lines A, B, C and data inputs D0..D7. What data values implement f(A,B,C)=Σm(1,2,5,7)?
quiz.a: Set D1=D2=D5=D7=1 and all other data inputs to 0. Then the mux output is 1 exactly for the listed minterms.

quiz.q: What does the high-impedance state of a tristate buffer mean, and why is it useful on a bus?
quiz.a: High-Z means the output is disconnected from the bus. Many drivers can share one bus if exactly one driver is enabled at a time.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, decoders and muxes appear as standard cells in every memory compiler and FPGA routing fabric. Comparators sit inside branch units, sorting accelerators and high-speed data converters. Search for 'address decoder', 'transmission gate multiplexer', and 'magnitude comparator Verilog' to go deeper.
